lead: Operators are matrices, and a calculation often needs not just A but A squared, a polynomial in A, a square root of A, or the exponential e^A. These are defined through the eigenvalues: keep the eigenvectors and push each eigenvalue through the ordinary function. For a Hermitian A written as A = Σ λ|λ⟩⟨λ|, the rule is f(A) = Σ f(λ)|λ⟩⟨λ|. One consequence runs through all of quantum mechanics: the time-evolution operator is the matrix exponential U(t) = e^(−iHt/ħ), and it is unitary.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and 1.5 for Hermitian and unitary matrices.

blocks.text: A square matrix A can be multiplied by itself: A² = AA, A³ = A²A, and A⁰ = I, the identity matrix. A polynomial in A means p(A) = a₀I + a₁A + a₂A² + ⋯ + a_d A<sup>d</sup> for p(x) = a₀ + a₁x + ⋯ + a_d x<sup>d</sup>. The constant term a₀ multiplies I; it never sits alone as the number a₀.

Infinite series extend the same way. For f(x) = Σ<sub>k</sub> c<sub>k</sub> x<sup>k</sup>, set f(A) = Σ<sub>k</sub> c<sub>k</sub> A<sup>k</sup>. So e<sup>A</sup> = I + A + A²/2! + A³/3! + ⋯, and sin A and cos A are defined by their series. The matrix series converges when the number series converges at every eigenvalue of A, so the eigenvalues decide whether f(A) exists.
Quantum computing uses these objects constantly: time evolution is an exponential of the energy operator, and rotation gates are exponentials of Pauli matrices (Unit 3).

items: Find the eigenvalues λ<sub>k</sub> and an orthonormal eigenbasis |λ<sub>k</sub>⟩ of A.
Check that f(λ<sub>k</sub>) is defined and finite at every eigenvalue.
Write A in spectral form A = Σ<sub>k</sub> λ<sub>k</sub>|λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>|.
Replace each λ<sub>k</sub> by f(λ<sub>k</sub>), giving f(A) = Σ<sub>k</sub> f(λ<sub>k</sub>)|λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>|.
Multiply out in the original basis if the answer must be a matrix.

blocks.text: A normal operator satisfies AA† = A†A; every Hermitian or unitary operator is normal. Such an operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis, so A = Σ<sub>k</sub> λ<sub>k</sub>|λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>|, where each P<sub>k</sub> = |λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>| is a projector: P<sub>k</sub>² = P<sub>k</sub>, P<sub>k</sub>P<sub>j</sub> = 0 for k ≠ j, and Σ<sub>k</sub> P<sub>k</sub> = I.

blocks.where: λ<sub>k</sub> are the eigenvalues of A; |λ<sub>k</sub>⟩ are the matching unit eigenvectors; f(λ<sub>k</sub>) is the ordinary function evaluated at the number λ<sub>k</sub>; the sum runs over all distinct eigenvalues.

blocks.text: Read the formula as a recipe. f never touches the eigenvectors; it only rescales each eigenvalue. So f(A) has the same eigenvectors as A, and its eigenvalues are f(λ<sub>k</sub>).

For a diagonal matrix the rule collapses to entry-by-entry work: if A = diag(λ₁, …, λ<sub>n</sub>), then f(A) = diag(f(λ₁), …, f(λ<sub>n</sub>)). This shortcut is valid only after you are in the eigenbasis.

items: tr f(A) = Σ<sub>k</sub> f(λ<sub>k</sub>) and det f(A) = Π<sub>k</sub> f(λ<sub>k</sub>).
If A is Hermitian and f is real on the real line, then f(A) is Hermitian.
If |f(λ<sub>k</sub>)| = 1 for every eigenvalue, then f(A) is unitary.
f(A) commutes with A, because both are diagonal in the same eigenbasis.

sections.h3: The matrix exponential and time evolution

blocks.text: The exponential is the most used operator function. Its series is e<sup>A</sup> = Σ<sub>k</sub> A<sup>k</sup>/k! = I + A + A²/2! + A³/3! + ⋯, with k! = 1·2·3⋯k. For a diagonal A you apply exp to each diagonal entry; for a general Hermitian A you use the spectral form.

blocks.where: H is the Hamiltonian, a Hermitian operator with units of energy (joules); t is time in seconds; ħ = h/2π = 1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s is the reduced Planck constant; i is the imaginary unit; U(t) is the dimensionless time-evolution operator.

blocks.text: Why is U(t) unitary? H is Hermitian, so its eigenvalues λ are real numbers. The eigenvalues of −iHt/ħ are then −iλt/ħ, which are purely imaginary, and each number e<sup>−iλt/ħ</sup> has modulus 1. By the rule above, U(t) has eigenvalues of modulus 1, so it is unitary. A unitary U keeps ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ unchanged, which is conservation of probability.

Two cautions. First, e<sup>A+B</sup> = e<sup>A</sup>e<sup>B</sup> only when AB = BA. Second, the sign carries meaning: e<sup>−iHt/ħ</sup> moves a state forward in time, and its adjoint e<sup>+iHt/ħ</sup> moves it backward.

examples.question: A two-dimensional operator is A = diag(0, π). (a) Write A in spectral form with its projectors. (b) Using operator functions, compute e^(iA). (c) Show that e^(iA) is unitary. (d) State the eigenvalues of e^(iA) and their moduli.
steps: A is diagonal, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: λ₁ = 0 with eigenvector |λ₁⟩ = (1, 0), and λ₂ = π with eigenvector |λ₂⟩ = (0, 1).
The projectors are P₁ = |λ₁⟩⟨λ₁| = diag(1, 0) and P₂ = |λ₂⟩⟨λ₂| = diag(0, 1). Spectral form: A = 0·P₁ + π·P₂.
Here f(x) = e^(ix). So f(λ₁) = e^(i·0) = cos 0 + i sin 0 = 1, and f(λ₂) = e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1 + 0i = −1.
Apply f to each eigenvalue: e^(iA) = 1·P₁ + (−1)·P₂ = diag(1, 0) + diag(0, −1) = diag(1, −1). On a diagonal matrix the same answer comes entry by entry: diag(e^(i0), e^(iπ)) = diag(1, −1).
Unitarity: (e^(iA))† = diag(1, −1) because both entries are real, so (e^(iA))†(e^(iA)) = diag(1·1, (−1)·(−1)) = diag(1, 1) = I.
The eigenvalues of e^(iA) are 1 and −1, and |1| = 1, |−1| = 1. Both moduli equal 1, which is the eigenvalue test for unitarity.
examples.answer: e^(iA) = diag(1, −1), which is unitary; its eigenvalues are 1 and −1, both of modulus 1.
examples.check:
import cmath
u1 = cmath.exp(1j * 0.0)
u2 = cmath.exp(1j * cmath.pi)
print(round(u1.real, 6))
print(round(u2.real, 6))
print(round(abs(u1), 6))
print(round(abs(u2), 6))

traps: Applying f entry by entry to a non-diagonal matrix. For X = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], entry-by-entry would give [[1, e], [e, 1]], which is wrong; the correct value is cosh(1)I + sinh(1)X.
Forgetting that the constant term of a polynomial multiplies I: p(A) = a₀I + a₁A + ⋯, never a₀ + a₁A + ⋯.
Writing time evolution as e^(−Ht/ħ) or e^(+iHt/ħ). The forward evolution is e^(−iHt/ħ); the plus sign gives the adjoint, which runs time backward.
Assuming e^(A+B) = e^A e^B always. It needs AB = BA, and most quantum operators do not commute.
Applying √ or log without checking the spectrum: √A needs every eigenvalue ≥ 0 and log A needs every eigenvalue > 0, otherwise f(λ) is not a finite number.

quiz.q: State the definition of f(A) for a Hermitian operator A and name each symbol.
quiz.a: With A = Σ λ<sub>k</sub>|λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>| over orthonormal eigenvectors, f(A) = Σ f(λ<sub>k</sub>)|λ<sub>k</sub>⟩⟨λ<sub>k</sub>|. λ<sub>k</sub> is an eigenvalue, |λ<sub>k</sub>⟩ its unit eigenvector, and f is applied to the number λ<sub>k</sub>.

quiz.q: Why can you not compute f(A) by applying f to each matrix entry when A is not diagonal?
quiz.a: Matrix entries depend on the chosen basis, and the off-diagonal entries carry the mixing action of A. Applying f entry by entry ignores that mixing and disagrees with the power series. The spectral rule is basis-independent and agrees with the series.

quiz.q: For A = diag(1, 4), compute A², √A and e<sup>A</sup>.
quiz.a: A² = diag(1², 4²) = diag(1, 16). √A = diag(√1, √4) = diag(1, 2). e<sup>A</sup> = diag(e¹, e⁴) ≈ diag(2.718, 54.598).

quiz.q: For A = diag(0, π/2), compute e<sup>iA</sup> and check unitarity.
quiz.a: e<sup>iA</sup> = diag(e<sup>i0</sup>, e<sup>iπ/2</sup>) = diag(1, i). Its adjoint is diag(1, −i), so the product is diag(1, (−i)(i)) = diag(1, 1) = I; the eigenvalues 1 and i both have modulus 1.

quiz.q: Show that U = e<sup>−iHt/ħ</sup> is unitary when H is Hermitian and t is real.
quiz.a: Write H = Σ λ|λ⟩⟨λ| with real λ, since H is Hermitian. Then U = Σ e<sup>−iλt/ħ</sup>|λ⟩⟨λ|. The exponent −λt/ħ is real, so each eigenvalue has modulus 1. Hence U†U = Σ |e<sup>−iλt/ħ</sup>|²|λ⟩⟨λ| = Σ |λ⟩⟨λ| = I.

quiz.q: For X = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] and real θ, show that e<sup>iθX</sup> = cos θ I + i sin θ X.
quiz.a: X has eigenvalues +1 and −1, so X = P₊ − P₋ with P₊ + P₋ = I. Apply f(x) = e<sup>iθx</sup>: e<sup>iθX</sup> = e<sup>iθ</sup>P₊ + e<sup>−iθ</sup>P₋ = cos θ (P₊ + P₋) + i sin θ (P₊ − P₋) = cos θ I + i sin θ X.

beyond: Not for the exam. Numerical libraries compute these operators with routines such as expm and sqrtm rather than by summing series, because series lose accuracy fast. Simulating e<sup>−iHt/ħ</sup> on a quantum computer uses Lie–Trotter–Suzuki product formulas, which are the workhorse of Hamiltonian simulation in research. The matrix logarithm of a density matrix gives the von Neumann entropy used in Unit 5, and functional calculus is a standard topic in operator theory courses. Search terms: matrix function, Spectral theorem functional calculus, Trotter–Suzuki decomposition, scipy.linalg.expm.
